record: GR00T N1.5 compiled (TensorRT fp16) on all three NVIDIA boards: per-stage engine times, each gated against an fp32 reference. On Orin, where our TensorRT major version matches NVIDIA's, our stage times agree with their published figures to 0.5%.

external_validation_vs_nvidia_published.source: NVIDIA, Isaac-GR00T deployment_scripts/README.md — 'Model latency measured by trtexec with batch_size=1', our exact method
external_validation_vs_nvidia_published.reading: Corrected 2026-08-27 (an earlier version of this field read 'every stage within 14% and 10.2% FASTER overall ... independent confirmation the harness is honest'). The Thor comparison is VERSION-MISMATCHED (our TensorRT 10.16.2 vs NVIDIA's ~10.3-era figures), so the 10.2% is toolchain drift, not superiority. The valid comparison is Orin, where the major version matches: NVIDIA's ViT 11.96 / LLM 17.25 / DiT 7.77 = 60.29 ms on our accounting against our measured 60.005 -- agreement to 0.5%, with per-stage deltas mixed in sign (+2.0% / -11.1% / +4.5%). Mixed signs on identically exported ONNX is what genuine agreement looks like, and it also rules out the objection that we measure less work. jetson_clocks: NVIDIA's ON, ours OFF.
external_validation_vs_nvidia_published.thor_row_is_not_a_validation: version-mismatched; retained for the record, not to be cited as agreement or as a win.

cross_board_compiled_stage_sum.accounting: ViT + LLM + 4 x DiT_step on every board. EXCLUDES vlln_vl_self_attention, action_encoder, state_encoder, action_decoder, and all CPU-side transforms/prep/post.

rows.trt: 10.16.1.11 (Python API — no trtexec on this host)

cross_board_compiled_stage_sum.headline: compiling cuts the ViT + LLM + 4 x DiT-step stage sum 3.0x (RTX 5090), 1.87x (Thor) and 3.72x (Orin) relative to PyTorch eager (eager_speedup).

compile_headroom_varies_by_board.mechanism: eager-to-compiled speed-up of the stage sum. At 2.72B parameters GR00T's eager kernels are already large, which limits what TensorRT's fusion can recover; and the headroom varies 2x across boards for the SAME model.
compile_headroom_varies_by_board.caveat: predicting one model's compiled time by applying another model's (or another board's) eager-to-compiled speed-up is not sound: such predictions missed both Orin (predicted 18-51 ms, measured 60.0) and Thor (predicted 18-25 ms, measured 31.95).

thor_dit_anomaly.what: Thor's DiT costs 4.944 ms — essentially the same as its own ViT (4.816) — whereas DiT is far cheaper than ViT on Orin (8.12 vs 12.20) and the 5090 (1.31 vs 1.82).
thor_dit_anomaly.magnitude: Thor's DiT is only 1.64x faster than Orin's, while its ViT is 2.53x faster and its LLM 2.05x.
thor_dit_anomaly.not_a_gate_failure: the engine is correct — cosine 0.99999 against a fresh reference, three independent builds agreeing to 0.48%.
thor_dit_anomaly.status: diagnosed later the same day: see thor_dit_anomaly_CLOSED_2026-08-27.json (DRAM-bandwidth roofline effect plus one mis-selected kernel). At the time of this record the kernel-level cause had not been diagnosed.

fp16_build_trap_reproduced_on_all_three_.symptom: plain --fp16 on the Qwen3 LLM prints '&&&& PASSED' with NO zeros, NO NaNs, a plausible value range and a plausible mean — while being structurally wrong. An all-zeros check passes it.
fp16_build_trap_reproduced_on_all_three_.detector: the FLOAT-tensor count in the engine's layer info. A correct build keeps 98 Float tensors (the RMSNorm fp32 regions); a broken one has ZERO. One number, unambiguous, and it flagged every broken build.
fp16_build_trap_reproduced_on_all_three_.speed_is_not_the_symptom: an earlier note read 'the broken build is FASTER, so the error flatters'. That does not generalise: it was 1.9% faster on Orin but 3.9% SLOWER on Thor and 0.2% slower on the 5090. Correctness is free on two of three boards. The trap is dangerous because it is SILENT, not because it is fast.

stored_dit_reference_offset.finding: the stored DiT reference gdit_ref.npy (and ref_dit.npy, a byte-copy) is NOT what onnxruntime-CPU produces from DiT_fp16.onnx. A fresh ORT run is bit-deterministic (run-to-run cosine exactly 1.0) yet differs from the stored reference by cosine 0.99754.
stored_dit_reference_offset.consequence: the DiT cosines previously reported for Orin (0.997764) are dominated by that REFERENCE OFFSET, not by accelerator error. Against a fresh reference the DiT engines score 0.99999 on both new boards.
stored_dit_reference_offset.scope: ViT and LLM are UNAFFECTED — stored and fresh references agree to 0.99999. NO TIMING IS AFFECTED. Fresh references saved at $GVRB_WORK/trtwork/freshref_{vit,llm,dit}.npy; both cosines are reported in the underlying records.
stored_dit_reference_offset.not_yet_done: the origin of the offset is not identified — whether the stored reference was produced by a different opset, a different ORT version, or a different graph revision.

method_and_rigour.thor_and_orin: median of THREE independent builds (Thor LLM spread 6.7%, consistent with the known TensorRT build-to-build variance floor — a single build would have misled)
method_and_rigour.rtx_5090: median of SIX builds; timed via cudaEvents bracketing execute_async_v3 only, matching trtexec's GPU Compute Time. Four independent methods agree: per-stage 9.091, sum-of-parts 9.0909, sequential 3-engine chain 9.0659, 20 s sustained 9.0888 — handoff cost -0.28%.
method_and_rigour.4x_dit_accounting_verified: measured 4-step DiT 5.1646 ms vs 4 x single-step 5.2236 (-1.13%), so the multiplication is fair
method_and_rigour.gating: every engine's output dumped and compared against an fp32 reference in the SAME invocation, on cosine as well as all-zero
method_and_rigour.config: jetson_clocks NOT applied on either Jetson; NVIDIA's published figures DO use it, so our comparison against them is conservative
method_and_rigour.5090_build_note: TensorRT's Python API refuses dynamic dims without an explicit optimization profile, where trtexec infers one from --minShapes. Fixed with min=opt=max matching Orin's shapes.

input_provenance: the exact stage-input tensors of the GR00T runs, captured from a recorded (simulated) GR1 observation in NVIDIA's demo_data/robot_sim.PickNPlace episode (not synthetic data), md5-verified identical across host and boards. Inputs were re-cast to each engine's binding dtypes (fp16 for tensors, int64 for position_ids/attention_mask/timesteps_tensor) -- feeding the raw fp32/int32 files would have made trtexec reinterpret the bytes and produce confident garbage.
title_corrected_2026-08-27: This record's title read '...and we beat NVIDIA's own published Thor figures by 10.2%' until 2026-08-27. That claim is withdrawn: our Thor runs use TensorRT 10.16.2 against NVIDIA's ~10.3-era figures, so the 10.2% is toolchain version drift, not harness superiority. Where the versions match (Orin, 10.3) the two agree to 0.5%, which is the stronger validation.
